title: Control valves
calcLabel: Open the control valve sizing calculator

steps.q: A control valve has a Kv of 10. What does that mean?
board: A control valve has a Kv
steps.title: Kv
steps.summary: Kv is the flow of water in m³/h through a valve with a 1 bar pressure drop across it. For other conditions, flow Q = Kv × √(ΔP ÷ SG), with Q in m³/h and ΔP in bar. Cv, the US equivalent in gallons per minute at 1 psi, is about 1.16 × Kv. Catalogue Kv values are for the fully open valve.

opts.t: 10 m³/h of water at 1 bar drop
10 bar pressure drop at full flow
10 litres a minute of any liquid

draw: Kv = m³/h of water at 1 bar ΔP

steps.q: Same valve opening, but the pressure drop across it rises 4 times. What happens to flow?
steps.title: Square root
steps.summary: At a fixed opening, flow through a valve goes with the square root of the pressure drop, so four times the pressure drop doubles the flow. Doubling the flow at the same opening would need four times the pressure drop, which is rarely available.

steps.q: A new control valve runs at only 10 % open at normal flow. What's the problem?
steps.title: Oversized valve
steps.summary: A valve running at only 10 % open is oversized. Near the seat small movements cause large flow changes, so control is jumpy, and high velocity through the small gap wears the seat and plug. Size the valve on real flows so the range from minimum to maximum flow sits within roughly 20 to 80 % open, with normal flow often around 50 to 70 %; control valves are often a size or two smaller than the line.

draw: size on flow, not pipe size

steps.q: The valve takes a small share of the system pressure drop. Which characteristic suits?
steps.title: Characteristic
steps.summary: A valve's characteristic is how flow changes with opening at constant pressure drop. In most systems pipe friction takes more pressure as flow rises, leaving less for the valve. An equal percentage characteristic opens slowly at first and faster later, which compensates, so the installed response is closer to linear. If the valve takes most of the system pressure drop, a linear characteristic suits better.

draw: more flow → less ΔP left for valve
valve takes most of drop → linear

steps.q: A liquid control valve sounds like gravel flowing through it. What's going on?
steps.title: Valve cavitation
steps.summary: Liquid accelerates through the narrowest gap in the valve and its pressure falls sharply. If it drops below the vapour pressure, bubbles form, then collapse as pressure recovers downstream, sounding like gravel and eroding the trim and nearby pipe. Fixes include sharing the pressure drop across two valves or an orifice, anti-cavitation trim, or locating the valve where pressure is higher.

steps.q: What does a valve positioner do?
steps.title: Positioner
steps.summary: Packing friction can stop a valve stem short of where the control signal wants it. A positioner compares the signal with the actual stem position and adds or vents actuator air until they match, reducing stick-slip and speeding response. Smart positioners also report travel and friction, helping spot a sticking valve early.

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: control valves, the hands of every control loop. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now size a valve in the control valve sizing calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. A control valve has a Kv of 10. What does that mean?

q1-r0.text: Yes! Water flow in cubic metres an hour at 1 bar across it.

q1-r1.text: Kv is a flow number, not a pressure drop.

q1-r2.text: Opening is separate. Kv is the valve's capacity.

q1-r3.text: Wrong units, and it's defined for water.

q1-b0.text: Kv is the flow of water, in cubic metres an hour, through the valve with 1 bar across it.

q1-b1.text: For other liquids and drops, flow equals Kv times the square root of pressure drop over specific gravity.

q1-b2.text: Cv is the American version, in gallons per minute at 1 psi. Cv is about 1.16 times Kv.

q1-b3.text: Catalogues quote the Kv at full open. You pick a valve whose normal flow needs only part of it.

q2.text: Question 2. Same valve opening, but the pressure drop across it rises 4 times. What happens to flow?

q2-r0.text: Flow goes with the square root of pressure drop.

q2-r2.text: More push, more flow. It changes.

q2-r3.text: More pressure drop pushes more flow, not less.

q2-b0.text: At a fixed opening, flow goes with the square root of the pressure drop, until the flow chokes.

q2-b1.text: Four times the pressure drop gives the square root of 4: twice the flow.

q2-b2.text: That's why the same valve opening gives different flows when the upstream pressure changes.

q2-b3.text: And to double the flow at the same opening, you'd need four times the pressure drop. Usually not available.

q3.text: Question 3. A new control valve runs at only 10 % open at normal flow. What's the problem?

q3-r0.text: Spare, yes. Controllable, no. It's working on the seat.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Tiny movements make big flow changes, and the seat wears.

q3-r2.text: Undersized valves run nearly wide open, not nearly shut.

q3-r3.text: The actuator is fine. The valve is too big.

q3-b0.text: At 10 percent open, a small stem movement is a big share of the opening, so flow jumps. Stem friction makes it worse.

q3-b1.text: High velocity through the small gap also wears the seat and the plug.

q3-b2.text: Aim to keep minimum to maximum flow within roughly 20 to 80 percent open. Normal flow often sits around 50 to 70.

q3-b3.text: Size the valve on real flows, not on the pipe size. Valves are often a size or two smaller than the line.

q4.text: Question 4. The valve takes a small share of the system pressure drop. Which characteristic suits?

q4-r0.text: Linear suits a valve that takes most of the drop. Not this one.

q4-r1.text: Quick opening is for on-off duty, not throttling.

q4-r2.text: Correct! It makes up for the shrinking pressure drop.

q4-r3.text: It matters a lot for how the loop behaves.

q4-b0.text: A characteristic is how flow changes with opening, with a constant drop across the valve.

q4-b1.text: In a real system, as flow rises, pipe friction takes more pressure, and less is left for the valve.

q4-b2.text: Equal percentage opens slowly at first and faster later, which cancels that effect. The installed response ends up near straight.

q4-b3.text: If the valve takes most of the system drop, linear is the better choice.

q5.text: Question 5. A liquid control valve sounds like gravel flowing through it. What's going on?

q5-r0.text: Probably not. It's bubbles, not stones.

q5-r1.text: Cavitation! Same villain as in pumps.

q5-r2.text: A loose actuator rattles differently. This is flow noise.

q5-r3.text: Gravel noise isn't normal. Something's collapsing in there.

q5-b0.text: Liquid speeds up through the narrowest gap, and its pressure drops sharply there.

q5-b1.text: If it falls below the vapour pressure, bubbles form. Then the pressure recovers downstream and they collapse.

q5-b2.text: The collapse sounds like gravel and eats the trim and the pipe just downstream.

q5-b3.text: Fixes: share the pressure drop across two valves or an orifice, use anti-cavitation trim, or put the valve where pressure is higher.

q6.text: Question 6. What does a valve positioner do?

q6-r1.text: Yes! It fights friction until the stem is in the right place.

q6-r2.text: Tuning lives in the controller, not on the valve.

q6-r3.text: The opposite. It keeps moving it to the right place.

q6-b0.text: Without a positioner, packing friction can stop the stem short of where the signal wants it.

q6-b1.text: The positioner compares the signal with the actual stem position and adds or vents air until they match.

q6-b2.text: Result: less stick-slip, faster response, and a valve that really goes to 37 percent when asked.

q6-b3.text: Smart positioners also report travel and friction, so you can spot a sticking valve early. Size your next valve in the control valve sizing calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
